summary: Kole Jain walks through three ways to price website design work: hourly, flat project pricing, and value-based pricing, which he calls the holy grail. He gives rough hourly rates by experience level (and notes they depend heavily on location), then shows how to build a project price from a break-even cost (estimated hours times hourly rate) marked up by a factor between 1 and 2 depending on how interesting and valuable the client is. Value-based pricing takes a share (5 to 10%) of the extra revenue a redesign produces, so prices scale with client size rather than time spent, but it only works when the result can be tied to a measurable revenue increase. This is freelance business advice rather than design guidance; for someone building a design system it matters mainly as a way to scope and price the work itself [inferred].
key_ideas: There are three pricing models for design work: hourly, project (flat rate) and value-based.
Hourly rates are very location specific; the video contrasts about $50 an hour in the US with about 12 in India.
Hourly billing sets designer and client against each other: one wants more hours billed, the other fewer.
Hourly pricing is useful only while you cannot yet price a project accurately.
Clients prefer a hard number up front, which project pricing gives them.
Project price starts from a break-even cost: estimated hours multiplied by your hourly rate.
Time estimates should also account for meetings and revisions.
Mark up the break-even by a factor between 1 and 2: close to 1 for a high-profile client who brings future work, higher for a dull client.
Value-based pricing takes a cut of the extra revenue your redesign creates, generally 5 to 10%.
Value-based pricing lets your price scale with client size regardless of hours spent, but requires estimating revenue gain and agreeing an ROI with the client.
Value-based pricing does not fit clients with no revenue or non-profits; fall back to project pricing.
Work usually takes longer than you expect, and your skills are worth more than you think.

rules.rule: Move from hourly to flat project pricing once you can estimate a project's scope.
rules.why: Hourly billing gives designer and client opposing incentives, and clients want a hard number up front; hourly is only useful while you cannot accurately price a project.
rules.evidence: quickly becomes counterproductive after that ... project pricing fixes all of that

rules.rule: Calculate a project's break-even cost by multiplying the estimated hours by your hourly rate.
rules.why: It is the base from which the flat project price is built.
rules.evidence: we calculate our break even cost by figuring out how long it's going to take and multiplying that by our hourly rate

rules.rule: Include time for meetings and revisions in every project time estimate.
rules.why: The time benchmarks are only guidelines, and things generally take longer than you think they will.
rules.evidence: don't forget to account for meetings and revisions as well

rules.rule: Multiply the break-even cost by a factor between 1 and 2 based on how interesting the project is and how much future value the client brings.
rules.why: A big-name client who will bring more clients is worth doing near break-even; a boring client should cost more for the same work.
rules.evidence: gross up our break even point ... by a factor of anywhere between 1 and two

rules.rule: For value-based pricing, charge a share of the additional revenue the redesign produces, generally 5 to 10%.
rules.why: The designer should get a piece of the extra profit the work creates, and this lets prices scale with larger clients regardless of time spent.
rules.evidence: value based pricing reckons that you should get a piece of this additional profit generally it's 5 to 10%

rules.rule: Do not use value-based pricing when the work cannot be tied to a quantifiable revenue increase, such as a client with no revenue or a non-profit; use project pricing instead.
rules.why: Value-based pricing depends on measuring the revenue gain.
rules.evidence: if for example the company isn't generating any revenue or maybe they're a non-for-profit this doesn't make much sense

rules.rule: Treat hourly-rate guidelines as location specific and adjust them to where you work.
rules.why: Designer pay is very location specific: about $50 an hour on average in the US versus about 12 in India.
rules.evidence: please note this is very location specific

rules.rule: If you do not know what to charge, use experience-based hourly guidelines (US and similar countries): 20 to $30 an hour after 1 to two years of designing, $35 to $50 after working with a few clients successfully, then 60 up to $100 after a year or so of that.
rules.why: The presenter offers these as guidelines for designers who don't know what to charge, with rates rising as experience and successful client work grow.
rules.evidence: after working with a few clients successfully you could bump that up to $35 to $50 an hour

rules.rule: For value-based pricing, estimate the client's revenue gain and agree an acceptable ROI with them before setting the fee.
rules.why: The fee is a share of that gain, so it has to be estimated; the presenter says there is no easy way around this extra complexity.
rules.evidence: now you need to estimate the gain in revenue and work with your client to figure out an acceptable Roi for them

rules.rule: When pricing, assume the work will take longer than you think and that your skills are worth more than you think.
rules.why: The presenter gives these as the two things to remember to price projects successfully and accurately.
rules.evidence: just remember these two things things generally take longer than you think they will

decisions.question: How should a design project be priced?

options.name: Hourly
options.effect: Bill for each hour worked; no concrete total, and designer and client pull in opposite directions on hours.
options.when: When you cannot yet accurately price out a project, typically early in your career.

options.name: Project (flat rate)
options.effect: One fixed price the client knows up front; easier for the client, more estimating work for the designer.
options.when: When you can estimate the hours, or as the fallback when value-based pricing does not apply.

options.name: Value-based
options.effect: Price is a share of the extra revenue the work generates, so fees scale with client size regardless of hours.
options.when: When the redesign can be tied to a quantifiable revenue increase and you can agree an acceptable ROI with the client.

decisions.recommendation: Value-based pricing is presented as the holy grail because prices scale with larger clients irrespective of time spent; project pricing is the fallback when revenue gain cannot be measured; hourly is only useful until you can price projects accurately.
decisions.evidence: the three types of pricing with the last one being the Holy Grail of pricing strategies

decisions.question: How much should the break-even cost be marked up for a given client?

options.name: About 1x (break-even)
options.effect: Charge roughly your cost and not much more.
options.when: A fantastic, big-name client who will likely bring you more clients.

options.name: 1.5x
options.when: A middle-of-the-road client who brings some value.

options.name: Up to 2x
options.effect: The highest markup for the same amount of work.
options.when: A really boring client; 2 is the top of the stated range.

decisions.recommendation: Scale the factor between 1 and 2 by how interesting the project is and how much future value the client brings.
decisions.evidence: consider how interesting this project is to us and how much value it's going to bring us in the future

process.detail: Base it on location and experience, e.g. $20 to $30 an hour for 1 to two years of designing in the US and similar countries, $35 to $50 after working with a few clients successfully, then 60 up to $100 after a year or so of that.
Estimate how long the project will take using benchmarks as guidelines, and add time for meetings and revisions.
Multiply the estimated hours by your hourly rate.
Judge how interesting the project is and how much future value (reputation, referrals) the client brings.
Multiply break-even by a factor between 1 and 2 to get the flat project price.

If the work ties to a quantifiable revenue increase, estimate the revenue gain, agree an acceptable ROI with the client, and charge a share of the gain (generally 5 to 10%); otherwise keep the project price.

examples.visual_note: A $4,000 break-even multiplied by 1.5 for a middle-of-the-road client gives a $6,000 project price.
A client making $2 million in revenue per year gains an additional 10% after a redesign; 5 to 10% of that gain equates to 10 to $20,000.

caveats: This is freelance business advice, not design guidance; it does not inform tokens, components or visual decisions [inferred].
Rates are rules of thumb from April 2024, given as location-specific guidelines for people who don't know what to charge; they are the presenter's opinion, not sourced data.
The video introduces 'common benchmarks for times' but they are not spoken in the transcript (presumably shown on screen [inferred]), so they are not captured here.
Auto-caption error: the transcript says 'break even point of $44,000', which almost certainly mis-hears the $4,000 break-even stated just before; the number is left out of the numbers list.
Short comedic interjections from an imagined client voice ('I'm getting it', 'passive income') are skits, not advice.
The presenter hopes you would no longer be charging hourly by the time you reach 60 to $100 an hour, implying hourly is a stage to move past.
